import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(14, 5.5))
ax.set_xlim(0, 14)
ax.set_ylim(0, 5.5)
ax.axis('off')

def rounded_box(ax, xy, width, height, text, facecolor='#F0F4F8', edgecolor='#4A5568',
                fontsize=10, fontweight='normal', text_color='#1A202C', linewidth=1.2,
                alpha=1.0, zorder=2):
    x, y = xy
    box = FancyBboxPatch((x, y), width, height,
                         boxstyle="round,pad=0.15",
                         facecolor=facecolor, edgecolor=edgecolor,
                         linewidth=linewidth, alpha=alpha, zorder=zorder)

    lines = text.split('\n')
    if len(lines) == 1:
        ax.text(x + width/2, y + height/2, text,
                ha='center', va='center', fontsize=fontsize,
                fontweight=fontweight, color=text_color, zorder=zorder+1)

        total_h = len(lines) * fontsize * 0.018
        for i, line in enumerate(lines):
            ly = y + height/2 + total_h/2 - i * fontsize * 0.018 - fontsize*0.009
            fw = fontweight
            if i == 0:
                fw = 'bold'
            ax.text(x + width/2, ly, line,
                    ha='center', va='center', fontsize=fontsize,
                    fontweight=fw, color=text_color, zorder=zorder+1)

def arrow(ax, start, end, color='#4A5568', lw=1.5):
    ax.annotate('', xy=end, xytext=start,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=color, lw=lw,
                                connectionstyle='arc3,rad=0'))

# Row positions

row_labels = ['CLS', 'CWM', 'TRAJ']

row_bg = ['#E8F0FE', '#FDE8D8', '#D4EDDA']
row_label_x = 0.15

# Column positions

input_w = 3.0
model_x = 5.6
model_w = 1.6
output_x = 8.0
output_w = 2.2
result_x = 11.0
result_w = 2.2

box_h = 1.2

for i, (ry, label, color, bg) in enumerate(zip(row_y, row_labels, row_colors, row_bg)):
    # Row label
    ax.text(row_label_x, ry + box_h/2, label,
            ha='center', va='center', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold',
            color=color, zorder=5,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.3', facecolor=bg, edgecolor=color, linewidth=2))

                    "Always\nparseable",

        arrow(ax, (output_x + output_w + 0.05, ry + box_h/2),

    elif i == 1:  # CWM

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

LLM-based automated program repair has advanced rapidly on real-world software tasks. Agent-based systems such as SWE-agent~\cite{yang2024sweagent} and pipeline approaches like Agentless~\cite{xia2024agentless} resolve substantial fractions of SWE-bench~\cite{jimenez2024swebench} issues through candidate patch generation and validation. The prevailing strategy for improving resolve rates is test-time compute scaling~\cite{snell2024scaling}: generating $K$ candidate patches and selecting the best via a verifier. This verification step is critical---without it, the additional compute invested in diverse patch generation yields diminishing returns, because correct patches are diluted among incorrect ones. Full execution verification---running the repository's test suite against each candidate---is reliable but expensive, costing \$1--3 and several minutes per candidate at repository scale\footnote{Based on per-instance costs reported by \citet{yang2024sweagent} and \citet{xia2024agentless}.}, making it prohibitive for large $K$. Two dominant paradigms have emerged. \textbf{Generation-based simulation}~\cite{meta2025cwm,maimon2026selfexecution} predicts execution output strings per test, deriving verdicts by exact match. This suffers three failure modes at scale: (1)~\emph{token-budget exhaustion} truncates long outputs; (2)~\emph{string-value errors} reject semantically correct outputs differing in surface form; (3)~\emph{format compliance collapse} renders the majority of predictions unparseable at repository-level complexity, with parseable accuracy dropping below chance (42--43\%).

\textbf{Trajectory-level scoring}~\cite{shum2025swerm} predicts patch-level correctness directly, bypassing generation. This is robust---no outputs to truncate or parse---but discards per-test diagnostic signals needed for targeted re-repair~\cite{yang2024sweagent,xia2024agentless}. The apparent trade-off: generation preserves per-test granularity at the cost of reliability, while trajectory-level scoring provides reliability at the cost of granularity.

We argue this trade-off is an artifact of the formulation. Per-test binary classification---predicting a single \textsc{Pass}/\textsc{Fail} token---eliminates all three failure modes by construction: a single-token output cannot be truncated, needs no string matching, and is always parseable, while preserving the per-test diagnostics that trajectory-level scoring discards. Prior learned verifiers (LEVER~\cite{ni2023lever}, CodeT~\cite{chen2023codet}) leverage execution signals but target candidate-level ranking rather than per-test diagnostic classification. No prior work compares classification and generation formulations at controlled model sizes across complexity levels.

Crucially, the advantage is complexity-dependent. At function level, both formulations achieve near-equivalent accuracy (\mbox{1.24\pp{}} gap, 5 seeds, 4B). The gap emerges only when \cwm{} failure modes dominate: at repository level, it widens to \mbox{25.59\pp{}}. We formalize this via an oracle accuracy-utility framework (\S\ref{sec:oracle}) that predicts when per-test granularity provides value given test distribution and prediction correlation.

We validate these predictions through controlled experiments comparing the three formulations on function-level benchmarks (HumanEval~\cite{chen2021humaneval} and MBPP~\cite{austin2021mbpp}) and repository-level tasks (SWE-bench Verified~\cite{chowdhury2024swebenchverified}), using Qwen3~\cite{qwen2025qwen3} models at 4B and 8B parameters with matched training data and compute. Figure~\ref{fig:reformulation} illustrates the three formulations. We make the following contributions:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
\item \textbf{Complexity-dependent reformulation advantage.} The \cls{}--\cwm{} gap grows with complexity: near-null at function level (\mbox{1.18\pp{}}, 4B), widening to 2.26\pp{} at 8B (bootstrap mean, $p = 0.0066$; both 3 seeds), and \mbox{25.59\pp{}} at repository level (4B-4B, seed~42), with a second \cwm{} seed confirming failure (59.09\%, seed~123). \item \textbf{Diagnostic granularity at equivalent accuracy.} Per-test classification achieves statistically equivalent variant-level accuracy to trajectory-level scoring (TOST equivalence test $p = 0.007$, $\pm$2\pp{} margin) while providing per-test diagnostic signals---which specific tests fail---at no accuracy cost. This enables downstream applications such as targeted re-repair that trajectory-level verifiers cannot support.
